As emphasized in Section 1.1, PSD and powder morphology testing are essential for characterizing recycled powder. The flowability and density of the powder are intimately linked to its morphology, with spherical powders providing optimal flowability and homogeneous layer packing [23]. Consequently, flowability and density have a direct impact on consistent layer deposition and lasing, ultimately leading to the fabrication of highly dense parts. Based on literature reviews and the collective experience of LANL, ORNL, and ANL, it is safe and cost- effective to recycle powder, provided that rigorous testing and data set practices are in place. Interstitial elements, such as oxygen, must be closely monitored in recycled batches, as various factors can contribute to their increase. While slight changes in oxidation levels may not negatively impact powder performance [21-22], significant increases in oxygen can ultimately compromise as-built material properties, underscoring the importance of periodic testing. To maintain powder quality, a refreshing procedure can be employed to keep all elements within acceptable ranges. This involves adding virgin powder to the used powder to control interstitial elements, such as oxygen and nitrogen, which may be present. Prior chemical analysis is necessary to determine the optimal amounts of virgin powder to be added, followed by a thorough blending method to mix the powders. It is essential to archive the amount of powder used, the refresh amount added, blending method and duration, and before and after chemical analysis in the data set for future reference. Refreshing and recycling must be performed with caution, as poor powder morphology and non-compliant alloy composition can lead to defects, increased surface roughness, and compromised properties. 1.1.3 Porosity and Voids Porosity and voids are common defects that can arise in fabricated parts, often as a result of inadequate fusion between layers, gas absorption, and keyholing. These defects can lead to a decrease in part density, ultimately compromising mechanical performance, particularly when subjected to fatigue loadings. Fortunately, these defects can be controlled and eliminated by optimizing processing parameters to achieve laser power stability and complete fusion. This is achieved by attaining an optimal energy density, characterized by a normal "convection mode" shaped melt pool, which ensures adequate penetration and overlap with previous layers and adjacent melt pools, respectively.
